title: Jewelry store controller's class presentation: accounting standards (GAAP, FASB, SEC), the AICPA, ongoing education and career skills
participant_role: Controller of a successful multi-location jewelry store (Master of Accountancy, aiming for CFO) planning a talk to a high school accounting class
judge_role: High school accounting teacher who invited the controller to speak to the class
scenario:
You are to assume the role of a controller of a successful jewelry store with multiple locations throughout the region. A high school accounting teacher (judge) has asked you to speak to the accounting class about the profession and wants to meet with you to discuss your presentation.

You graduated college with a Master of Accountancy 10 years ago and worked your way up from an accounts payable manager at the jewelry store to controller. You have your sights set on one day reaching the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) position.

You are excited to share your knowledge of the profession with high school students. The teacher (judge) has asked you to discuss specific topics to include accounting regulations and professional organizations.

You are to plan a brief presentation that covers the following:
- Standard Setting Bodies and Accounting Regulation, include GAAP, FASB, SEC
- Professional organizations, to include the AICPA
- Ongoing education in the profession
- Skills needed to enhance career progression

You are to define each and explain how each affects the accounting profession and the companies that accountants work with.

You will present an outline of your presentation to the teacher (judge) in a role-play to take place in the teacher's (judge's) office. The teacher (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear the presentation. After you have presented the information and have answered the teacher's (judge's) questions, the teacher (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

solution.overview: A strong answer defines GAAP as the principles that make financial reporting consistent and comparable, FASB as the body that writes GAAP, the SEC as the federal agency that regulates public companies and receives their audited statements, and the PCAOB (created by Sarbanes-Oxley) as the overseer of public company audits. It describes the AICPA as the CPA association that sets ethics standards and the CPA exam, names other organizations, then explains why accountants need continuing education (CPE, changing standards, technology) and which skills (technical, analytical, communication, leadership, technology) move someone from AP manager to controller to CFO.

by_task.task: Standard setting bodies and accounting regulation
answer: GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles): the principles, standards and procedures for financial accounting that improve consistency and comparability of financial reports

GAAP must be used when auditing publicly traded companies and is followed by most companies that obtain credit, so accountants must know its principles, assumptions and constraints and keep up with changes
FASB (Financial Accounting Standards Board): the professional organization that develops GAAP
SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission): independent federal agency that regulates publicly traded corporations and the securities industry and receives the financial statements audited by CPAs
PCAOB (Public Company Accounting Oversight Board): created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) to oversee audits of public companies; auditors must follow SOX rules
Effect on companies: even a private jewelry store follows GAAP so its bank and investors can trust and compare its statements
AICPA (American Institute of Certified Public Accountants): the CPA member association that develops ethical standards and the Uniform CPA Exam; accountants look to it for guidance on ethical matters
Other organizations: Accounting and Finance Women's Alliance, Institute of Management Accountants (IMA), National Association of Black Accountants, Institute of Internal Auditors, state CPA societies
Services they provide: certifications (CPA, CMA, CIA), continuing education courses, networking, technical guidance, career resources and advocacy
Membership signals professionalism to employers and clients and keeps the accountant connected to changes in the field
Licensed CPAs must complete continuing professional education (CPE) hours every reporting period to keep their license
Standards change constantly (new FASB updates, tax law changes), so accountants must keep learning to stay compliant
Technology such as cloud accounting, data analytics and automation changes how the work is done
Ongoing education also opens doors to promotion: a master's degree and the CPA helped move from AP manager to controller, and the CFO goal requires more

by_task.task: Skills needed to enhance career progression
answer: Technical accounting knowledge (GAAP, tax, internal controls) and credentials such as the CPA
Analytical and problem-solving skills to interpret numbers and advise management
Communication and presentation skills to explain financial results to non-accountants, owners and boards
Leadership, teamwork and ethics: managing staff in AP, then the whole accounting department as controller
Technology and software skills (accounting systems, Excel, data tools) and business strategy knowledge for the CFO role

judge_question_answers.question: What is a good entry-level job in accounting?
answer: Accounts payable or accounts receivable clerk, bookkeeper or staff accountant at a company; that is the path I took, starting in accounts payable
Staff auditor or tax associate at a CPA firm, which gives broad exposure to many businesses
Internships during college are a great way to get the first role and build toward the CPA exam

judge_question_answers.question: What types of businesses need accounting professionals?
answer: Every type: retailers like our jewelry store, manufacturers, service companies, banks and technology firms
Government agencies, non-profits, schools and hospitals also need accountants
CPA firms serve all of these with audit, tax and consulting work, so accounting jobs exist in every industry and region

key_concepts.definition: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles: the set of principles, standards and procedures that make financial statements consistent and comparable across companies.
Financial Accounting Standards Board: the private, independent organization that develops and updates GAAP in the United States.
Securities and Exchange Commission: the independent federal agency that regulates publicly traded companies and the securities markets and requires audited financial statements.
Public Company Accounting Oversight Board: created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 to oversee and inspect the auditors of public companies.
A 2002 federal law passed after major accounting scandals that tightened rules on financial reporting, internal controls and audits of public companies.
American Institute of Certified Public Accountants: the national association of CPAs that sets ethical standards for the profession and develops the Uniform CPA Exam.
Certified Public Accountant: a licensed accountant who passed the CPA exam and met education and experience requirements; only CPAs can audit financial statements.
Required ongoing training hours that CPAs must complete to keep their license current and stay up to date on standards and tax law.
The head of a company's accounting department, responsible for financial records, reporting and internal controls; often reports to the CFO.
The top finance executive who oversees accounting, budgeting, financing and financial strategy for the whole company.
A member association for a profession (AICPA, IMA, IIA, state CPA societies) that offers certifications, education, ethics guidance and networking.
Rules of integrity, objectivity, independence and confidentiality (set by the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct) that accountants must follow so financial information can be trusted.
